passages.t: ‘Not to us, O LORD, not to us’, and idols that cannot speak
passages.happening:
Psalm 115 begins by turning attention away from the people singing it. “Not to us, O LORD, not to us, but to Your name be the glory, because of Your loving devotion, because of Your faithfulness” (verse 1).

Other nations are mocking. “Why should the nations say, ‘Where is their God?’” (verse 2). The answer is short. “Our God is in heaven; He does as He pleases” (verse 3).

Then the psalm turns the question around. Where are their gods? “Their idols are silver and gold, made by the hands of men” (verse 4). The list that follows is almost funny. “They have mouths, but cannot speak; they have eyes, but cannot see” (verse 5). They have ears and noses, hands and feet, but none of them work (verses 6 and 7). The idols are so lifeless that “they cannot even clear their throats” (verse 7).

Then the warning. “Those who make them become like them, as do all who trust in them” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The nations' taunt, ‘Where is their God?’, is heard elsewhere in the Psalms when Israel had been defeated or shamed (Psalm 79:10). Many scholars think this psalm comes from after the exile, when Israel was small and weak among large empires with grand temples.

In the ancient world, the people who worshipped idols did not think of them as mere statues. Images were made with great care, often of wood covered with gold and silver. Special rites were held to make the god live in the image. Priests fed it, clothed it and washed it. Psalm 115 laughs at all of this. The idol has a mouth, and it is silent.

Israel's God had no image. He spoke, saw and heard. That difference is the whole point of the psalm.

Verse 8 is the sharpest line. People become like what they worship. Trust a thing that cannot see or hear or speak, and you will slowly lose the power to see and hear and speak truly yourself.
passages.later:
The prophets mocked idols in the same way. Isaiah wrote, “All makers of idols are nothing, and the things they treasure are worthless” (Isaiah 44:9). Jeremiah said idols are “Like scarecrows in a cucumber patch” (Jeremiah 10:5).

Paul told the people of Athens, “we should not think that the Divine Being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by man's skill and imagination” (Acts 17:29). And he named a less obvious idol: “greed, which is idolatry” (Colossians 3:5).

The last line of John's first letter is, “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (1 John 5:21).
passages.asks:
Few people today bow to statues. But anything we trust to save us, or make us worth something, can work like an idol: money, success, a person, a cause, a screen. Verse 8 asks what you are becoming like.

And verse 1 asks whose glory you are after. ‘Not to us’ is a hard prayer for anyone. It is a good one to say slowly, and often.

passages.t: ‘O Israel, trust in the LORD’, and ‘we will bless the LORD’
passages.happening:
Now three groups are called to trust. “O Israel, trust in the LORD! He is their help and shield” (verse 9). The same call goes to “O house of Aaron” (verse 10) and to “You who fear the LORD” (verse 11). Each time the answer comes back: ‘He is their help and shield.’

Then the psalm promises blessing to the same three groups (verses 12 and 13), “small and great alike” (verse 13). It prays, “May the LORD give you increase, both you and your children” (verse 14), and, “May you be blessed by the LORD, the Maker of heaven and earth” (verse 15).

The heavens belong to God, “but the earth He has given to mankind” (verse 16). Then: “It is not the dead who praise the LORD, nor any who descend into silence. But it is we who will bless the LORD, both now and forevermore. Hallelujah!” (verses 17 and 18).
passages.hearers:
The three calls sound like worship in the temple. A leader may have called out each line and a choir answered. ‘The house of Aaron’ is the priests. ‘Those who fear the LORD’ may mean all Israel, summed up. Or it may mean people from other nations who had come to worship Israel's God. Both readings are held.

A ‘shield’ was a soldier's protection in battle. To call God ‘help and shield’ is to say he stands between his people and harm.

Verse 17 reflects how much of the Old Testament speaks of death. The dead go down to silence and no longer join the praise of God's people. The book page's part on Sheol explains this, and how the hope of life after death grows brighter later in the Bible. Psalm 115 uses the silence of the grave to say something urgent to the living: praise God now, while you have breath.

Notice the contrast with the idols. They have mouths but cannot speak. The living people of God have mouths, and they use them to bless the LORD.
passages.later:
Psalm 135 repeats the lines about idols almost word for word (Psalm 135:15-18).

The New Testament speaks of a hope beyond the silence of verse 17: “But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20).
passages.asks:
The psalm's answer to empty idols is not an argument. It is trust and praise. Whoever you are, small or great, Israelite or one who has come from far away, the call is the same: trust the LORD.

And use your voice while you have it. Verse 18 says, ‘it is we who will bless the LORD.’ Not some day. Now.
